issues.legal_issue: A suit for a bare injunction is sufficient when the plaintiff is in lawful possession and faces interference or a threat, without a cloud over the plaintiff’s title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a permanent injunction on the basis that they were in possession of vacant sites and the defendant had interfered with that possession.
The defendant disputed both their possession and their title.
issues.conclusion: A plaintiff in lawful or peaceful possession whose possession is interfered with or threatened may sue for an injunction simpliciter if the title is not disputed or under a cloud.
issues.legal_principle: A person in lawful or peaceful possession may protect that possession against interference by seeking a prohibitory injunction, but a person in wrongful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the rightful owner. The court decides a bare-injunction claim by reference to possession, although title may arise incidentally or collaterally.

rule.if: injunction_suit and plaintiff_lawfully_possessed and interference_or_threat and title_not_clouded

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning immovable property.
predicates.plaintiff_lawfully_possessed: The claimant was in lawful or peaceful possession of the property.
predicates.interference_or_threat: The opposing party interfered with or threatened the claimant’s possession.
predicates.title_not_clouded: The opposing party’s claim did not raise a cloud over the claimant’s title.

issues.definition: When an injunction suit concerns property lawfully possessed by the claimant, interference or a threat is present, and title is not clouded, a bare injunction is sufficient.

issues.legal_issue: An injunction alone is insufficient when the claimant is out of possession or the claimant’s title is under a cloud.
material_facts: The suit property was a vacant site, and the first appellate court found that the defendant was in possession and that the plaintiffs had not established their title or possession.
The defendant claimed the property under a registered sale from the person accepted by both sides as its original owner, while the plaintiffs claimed through a purported oral gift to their vendor.
The plaintiffs’ vendor had no title deed or municipal mutation supporting her claimed title, and the parties presented conflicting accounts of how she acquired the property.
The plaintiffs did not amend their claim to seek a declaration after the defendant specifically disputed their title.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs should have brought a suit for declaration of title and consequential relief, including possession if required; a bare injunction suit was not the appropriate remedy on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Where the plaintiff is out of possession, the plaintiff must seek possession, with an injunction if necessary. Where title is disputed or under a cloud, declaratory relief is necessary; if the plaintiff is also out of possession, the plaintiff must seek declaration, possession, and any appropriate injunction. A cloud exists where an apparent defect in the plaintiff’s title or a prima facie right of a third party is shown. If a defendant’s defence raises a serious title dispute in a bare-injunction suit, the plaintiff may amend the claim or withdraw it with permission to bring a comprehensive suit.

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning immovable property.
predicates.plaintiff_out_of_possession: The claimant was not in possession of the property or could not establish possession.
predicates.title_clouded: An apparent defect in the claimant’s title or a prima facie competing right was shown.

issues.definition: When an injunction suit is brought by a claimant who is out of possession or whose title is clouded, an injunction alone is insufficient.

issues.legal_issue: In a bare-injunction suit concerning a vacant site, title may be examined to determine possession only when the title issue is properly raised and is simple; a complex or unpleaded title dispute belongs in a comprehensive title suit.
material_facts: The property was a vacant site, so physical use or occupation did not resolve who possessed it.
The plaintiffs’ claimed possession depended on their title through an alleged oral gift and the claimed protection of an ostensible owner transfer.
The defendant claimed through the person both sides accepted as the original owner, and the evidence and title theories were disputed.
The plaint did not plead the alleged oral gift or the facts needed for protection as a transfer from an ostensible owner, and no title issue was framed.
issues.conclusion: The court should not decide the disputed title in this injunction suit; the plaintiffs’ remedy was a comprehensive suit for declaration and consequential relief.
issues.legal_principle: For a vacant site, possession follows title, so title may need to be determined as a prelude to deciding de jure possession. A court may decide title in an injunction suit when the issue is straightforward and the necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue exist. It should relegate the parties to a comprehensive declaratory suit where title involves complicated questions of fact or law, or where the parties did not proceed on the basis that title was at issue. A title finding requires necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue, whether express or implied. The judgment discusses Vanagiri Sri Selliamman Ayyanar Uthirasomasundareswarar Temple v. Rajanga Asari, Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Annaimuthu Thevar v. Alagammal, and Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer in explaining the treatment of title in injunction suits.

rule.if: injunction_suit and vacant_site and title_needed_to_determine_possession and (title_issue_complicated or not title_properly_pleaded_and_raised)

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning immovable property.
predicates.vacant_site: The property was vacant and its possession was not established through physical occupation or use.
predicates.title_needed_to_determine_possession: Determining who had possession required determining who had title.
predicates.title_issue_complicated: The title dispute involved complicated questions of fact or law.
predicates.title_properly_pleaded_and_raised: The pleadings and an express or implied issue placed title before the court for determination.

issues.definition: When possession of a vacant site depends on title, a complicated title dispute or the absence of properly pleaded and raised title issues means the parties should pursue a comprehensive title suit.

issues.legal_issue: A title finding in an earlier injunction suit can bar a later title suit only when title was directly and substantially in issue and its determination was necessary to the earlier judgment.
material_facts: In this case, the plaint did not plead the alleged oral gift or the facts supporting the claimed ostensible ownership, and no issue on title was framed.
The High Court nevertheless made findings on title in the injunction suit; the Supreme Court held that those findings could not be made in the absence of the necessary pleadings and issue.
issues.conclusion: An incidental or collateral title finding does not operate as res judicata when title was not necessary to decide possession; a title finding may do so when title was directly and substantially in issue and necessary to the judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The court reconciled Vanagiri Sri Selliamman Ayyanar Uthirasomasundareswarar Temple v. Rajanga Asari with Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, as explained in Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer and reiterated in Annaimuthu Thevar v. Alagammal. A later suit is barred only where title was pleaded, an issue on title was raised, evidence was led, and the court decided title because that determination was necessary to its judgment.

rule.if: earlier_injunction_suit and title_pleaded_and_issued and title_finding_necessary and title_decision_final

predicates.earlier_injunction_suit: A party previously brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning the property.
predicates.title_pleaded_and_issued: The parties pleaded title and an express or implied issue on title was before the court.
predicates.title_finding_necessary: The court had to decide title to determine the claim for possession or injunction.
predicates.title_decision_final: The court’s decision on title attained finality.

issues.definition: When an earlier injunction suit placed title in issue, required a title determination, and produced a final decision, that title finding can bar a later title suit.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot reverse a decision by re-examining factual title disputes that were not pleaded or made the subject of an issue.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the plaintiffs had not established title or possession and concluded that a bare-injunction suit was not maintainable on the facts.
The High Court reversed that decision after finding an oral gift and applying the law on ostensible ownership, although the plaint contained no necessary pleadings and no title issue had been framed.
The Supreme Court found that the first appellate court’s judgment was well reasoned and that the High Court’s title findings concerned factual and legal matters not properly before it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure by re-examining facts, considering unpleaded matters not covered by an issue, formulating questions of law that did not arise, and interfering with the first appellate court’s judgment. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court judgment and dismissed the suit without deciding title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal is confined to substantial questions of law arising for consideration on the pleadings and issues. A court cannot investigate a title theory in the absence of necessary pleadings and an issue, and evidence or argument cannot substitute for them. The alleged oral gift and the claimed protection under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act involved mixed questions of fact and law; the necessary allegations and issues were absent.

rule.if: second_appeal and high_court_reexamined_facts and high_court_decided_unpleaded_title_matters and no_title_issue_framed

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made by a High Court hearing a second appeal.
predicates.high_court_reexamined_facts: The High Court reassessed factual findings made by the first appellate court.
predicates.high_court_decided_unpleaded_title_matte: The High Court decided a title theory that was not supported by the necessary pleadings.
predicates.no_title_issue_framed: No issue on title was framed for adjudication.

issues.definition: When a High Court in a second appeal reassesses facts and decides an unpleaded title dispute without a title issue, it exceeds its second-appeal jurisdiction.
